To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the bright and massive BOSS galaxies at z≈0.5 are evolving slowly (of the order 2±1.5 per ccent Gyr−1), that any possible flux excess from potentially unresolved objects is less than 1per cent in the rest-frame g band, and that the weighted large-scale clustering of the reddest BO SS galaxies is consistent with dynam ical passive evolution.

the BOSS galaxies that have the highest likelihood to be progenitors of LRGs are slowly evolving (by 2 ± 2 per cent Gyr − 1) by merging and that they evolve in a manner consistent with passive evolution.
the BOSS galaxies are slowly evolving (of order 2 per cent per Gyr by merging) with respect to LRGs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of massive, red, slowly evolving, and passively evolving galaxies, and the study of the evolution of the clustering in this population.
the evolution of the most massive galaxies and the evolution of their large-scale clustering.

the study of the progenitors of the most massive galaxies at low redshifts and with the identification of a sample of massive galaxies that is as clean as possible and that has evolved without major mergers, and that can be used for cosmological applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BOSS galaxies targeted here have a very low probability (less than 2 per cent for the most massive galaxies) of being a star-forming galaxy at z= 2.
our likelihoods provide a clean sample, with no significant contamination, that is close to passive evolution.
the BOSS galaxies are a mixture of passive and active galaxies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BOSS galaxies targeted by our analysis are the most passive and massive galaxies up to z≃ 0.7, and that our results are consistent with dynamical evolution of these galaxies.
the BOSS galaxy sample is a good proxy for the LRGs sample, and that the BOSS sample is a good tracer of the underlying dark matter distribution.

we have identified a population of galaxies, that is evolving slowly in terms of luminosity and clustering, that is as clean as possible, and as close to the ideal case of passive evolution as possible, and we have shown that this population is robust to different assumptions on the stellar population synthesis models.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, by using the stellar population synthesis modelling of galaxies in SDSS-I/ II and SDSS- III, we can infer the properties of galaxies in the BOSS survey and identify a sample that is as close to passive as possible, and which can be used for cosmological studies.
the BOSS galaxy sample can be used to study the growth of structure at z≈0.55 in a similar way to the LRG sample at z≈.0.3.
the LRGs are a fossil record of a slowly evolving galaxy population, and that the BOSS galaxies are a good sample for cosmological studies, provided that the weighting is applied correctly.
